# CALM Proxy — results

*Generated by `python -m bench_agent.make_results_md` on 2026-09-20 13:34 UTC. Every figure is read from the run directory named beside it; none is typed by hand.*

**What it is.** A proxy that sits between any coding agent and a local model server (Ollama / vLLM / llama.cpp). It records every request, shows where the prompt cache is being missed and why, and shortens the prompts that are safe to shorten — without changing the agent.

**Setup.** qwen2.5-coder:7b on a MacBook Air M4 (16 GB), agent = mini-swe, 10 ClassEval classes repackaged as standalone repos, Ollama 0.21.2 at `NUM_PARALLEL=1 CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768`.

---

## The headline

**Content-addressed dedup cut prompt tokens 37% and server time 2.12x (2495 s → 1176 s), with solve rate unchanged.**

- Measured over **all 10 conversations** the benchmark recorded (149 requests), replayed with the agent removed so the lever is the only variable.
- Per conversation: **0.99x to 3.67x**, median 1.55x, and **4 of 10 show no effect at all**.
- Solve rate: **4/10 vs 4/10**, discordant pairs 1–1, exact McNemar **p = 1.000**.

> The maximum on its own would be a sales pitch. The distribution is in §5. Source: `runs/20260920T091729Z_replay_sweep`, `runs/20260920T072732Z_ab_off`, `runs/20260920T072732Z_ab_on`.

---

## 1. A prompt-cache hit is worth 100x — and the server will not tell you when you got one

| | prompt evaluation | per prompt token |
|---|---|---|
| cold prefix | 25,711 ms | 5.956 ms |
| warm prefix | **253 ms** | **0.059 ms** |

**100.9x on prompt evaluation** for a 4,317-token prompt.

Two ways to throw it away, both measured in the same run:

- a **timestamp at the front of the system prompt**: 28,586 ms
- **one interleaved request** with a different prefix: 27,327 ms — with one KV slot, an agent that alternates between two prompt shapes evicts its own cache every switch

**The plan's headline metric does not exist.** Ollama reports no `cached_tokens` at all, and `prompt_eval_count` does not shrink on a hit, so "prompt tokens computed = prompt − cached" is unreadable on this server. Wall clock is the only instrument there is, which is why every number in this document is a time.

Source: `runs/20260920T063803Z_cache_probe`

## 2. Three of four candidate levers were killed by their own measurements — before being built

| lever | measured headroom | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| I-2 prefix-lint | **0.0 s** — churn tokens: 0 | killed |
| I-3 memo | **0.0 s** — 0 duplicate request keys of 42 | killed |
| I-4 dedup | 102.3 s of uncached duplicate bytes | **shipped** |
| I-5 `calm-run` | 2 reruns of 5 test commands, ~20 ms each | not built |

Sized from 42 real requests **before any lever was written**, so the choice was made on data rather than on a guess.

**Why I-2 scored zero, which is a result and not a disappointment.** The agent only ever *appends* to its transcript — it never stamps, reorders or rewrites it — so there is no churn to lint. Measured prefill across those requests was 283.3 s against 185.8 s for a perfect cache and 2,072.7 s for none: **the cache already captures 94.8% of what there is to capture.** A lint promising to win that back would be selling something already owned.

The agent sent **347,775 prompt tokens to get 4,514 completion tokens back** — a 77:1 ratio.

Source: `runs/20260920T074436Z_headroom`

## 3. So why does the agent keep getting slower? Context is not free

Measured request time fitted against both kinds of token, each with its own attention term (**r² = 0.975**, 73 requests):

```
done_ms = a*new + b*new*ctx + c*completion + d*completion*ctx
```

| | at 1,246 context | at 27,449 context | multiple |
|---|---|---|---|
| one prompt token | 7.36 ms | 16.04 ms | **2.18x** |
| one output token | 45.92 ms | 113.68 ms | **2.48x** |

Generation falls from ~22 tok/s to ~9 tok/s with nothing changed but the length of the transcript. **No prefix cache addresses this** — those tokens *are* cached, and are still attended to by every token generated. This is the argument for dedup, and it is not the argument we started with.

**Two independent checks the fit was never given:** `a` = 6.952 ms per prompt token against the cache probe's separately measured **5.96 ms**, and `c` = 42.697 ms per output token = **23 tok/s** against this model's known ~20 tok/s.

Source: `runs/20260920T072921Z_context_cost`

## 4. Run the same task twice and the two runs share 13.7% of their prompt

Same tasks, same agent, same settings, an hour apart (6 conversations):

- median prefix reusable from the previous run: **13.7%**
- **every** conversation diverges at **message 3**, cause: timestamp in tool output

The entire difference is one line of `ls -la` output:

```
run A:  ...3:03 .. | -rw-r--r--@ 1 justinzhang  staff   851 Sep 20 02:56 TA
run B:  ...3:27 .. | -rw-r--r--@ 1 justinzhang  staff   851 Sep 20 02:56 TA
```

**Caveat, and it must travel with the number:** that line is the *parent temp directory's* mtime, which our own harness creates fresh per task. **The trigger is ours, not a real repository's.** What this shows exactly is the mechanism — one volatile line 40 tokens in costs everything behind it, because a prefix cache is a prefix cache. A real repo churns something else (edited files' mtimes, `git status`, test durations) and the wall arrives later and costs less.

It also explains why two temperature-0 runs diverge: **the model is deterministic, the environment is not.** Assistant turn 0 is byte-identical across both runs; turn 1 differs because its prompt does, by six characters.

Source: `runs/20260920T080936Z_cross_run`

## 5. The lever measured with the agent taken out of the loop

**Why the A/B cannot size this.** At temperature 0 the agent is deterministic *given its prompt*, so the first message the lever rewrites forks the trajectory and the two arms become different agents taking different numbers of turns. A run ending at 127 s instead of the 480 s cap usually means the agent gave up early, not that tokens got cheaper.

So the replay bench removes the agent: it replays the requests a recorded run really sent, once with the lever off and once on, changing nothing else, and does that for **every** conversation rather than the flattering one.

| conversation | requests | prompt tokens | server time, off → on | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 25 | 305,232 → 117,984 (61%) | 469.0 s → 128.0 s | **3.67x** |
| 1 | 25 | 99,633 → 71,418 (28%) | 300.3 s → 121.3 s | **2.48x** |
| 3 | 22 | 285,283 → 177,859 (38%) | 499.6 s → 202.9 s | **2.46x** |
| 5 | 14 | 151,169 → 90,189 (40%) | 415.5 s → 173.3 s | **2.40x** |
| 4 | 17 | 214,701 → 163,549 (24%) | 485.2 s → 250.6 s | **1.94x** |
| 0 | 25 | 169,163 → 133,871 (21%) | 161.5 s → 137.5 s | **1.17x** |
| 7 | 5 | 14,086 → 14,086 (0%) | 41.2 s → 40.5 s | **1.02x** |
| 6 | 6 | 9,996 → 9,996 (0%) | 43.8 s → 43.4 s | **1.01x** |
| 8 | 5 | 12,423 → 12,423 (0%) | 45.5 s → 45.4 s | **1.00x** |
| 9 | 5 | 7,540 → 7,540 (0%) | 33.2 s → 33.5 s | **0.99x** |

**Pooled: 2495 s → 1176 s = 2.12x on 37% fewer prompt tokens.** Median 1.55x.

**4 of 10 conversations show no effect**, and they are all the short ones — five or six requests, nothing repeated yet. One comes out at 0.99x, marginally *slower*: that is the hashing the lever does for no return, and it is in the table.

> **The honest shape of the lever:** it does nothing when you do not need it, costs about 1% when it does nothing, and returns 2–3.7x on the long looping runs that were burning the time.

**Cross-checks.** The same long conversation was replayed separately in *both* arm orders: the orders agreed to within 4%, and it scored 3.61–3.69x there against **3.67x** in this sweep — a separate invocation, an hour apart, same answer. That is the best evidence available that these replays measure the lever and not the machine.

Restricted to **prompt processing alone** (generation capped at one token), the same conversation gives 6.95–7.18x. The full-decode figure is lower because decode is a large fixed cost the lever cannot remove; it is the one quoted everywhere here, because it is what a user actually waits for.

Source: `runs/20260920T091729Z_replay_sweep`, `runs/20260920T085217Z_replay_full`, `runs/20260920T083923Z_replay_prefill`

## 6. Does it survive contact with a real agent?

10 tasks, interleaved, one at a time, cap 480 s:

| task | dedup off | dedup on |
|---|---|---|
| ClassEval_10 | not solved (480 s) | not solved (127 s) |
| ClassEval_24 | solved (40 s) | solved (38 s) |
| ClassEval_27 | not solved (182 s) | solved (50 s) |
| ClassEval_3 | not solved (476 s) | not solved (162 s) |
| ClassEval_33 | not solved (480 s) | not solved (480 s) |
| ClassEval_35 | not solved (480 s) | not solved (354 s) |
| ClassEval_37 | not solved (307 s) | not solved (80 s) |
| ClassEval_47 | solved (46 s) | solved (45 s) |
| ClassEval_6 | solved (42 s) | not solved (130 s) |
| ClassEval_7 | solved (35 s) | solved (32 s) |

**4/10 vs 4/10 solved. Discordant pairs 1–1. Exact McNemar p = 1.000.** The contract's guard was that the lever must not cost solves. It does not.

**The total wall-clock column of this A/B is not evidence about the lever**, and the generated report says so inside the table rather than in a footnote. With 10 tasks this test can only detect a large difference; a one- or two-task gap is not evidence either way.

Source: `runs/20260920T072732Z_ab_off`, `runs/20260920T072732Z_ab_on`, full table in `results/proxy.md`

## What this does *not* claim

- **Not that we made the cache work better.** This agent's cache already captures 94.8% of what there is. The proxy *proved* that, and measured the cliff waiting for an agent whose prompt is not append-only.
- **Not that dedup saves 620 s of prefill.** Most bytes it removes were already cached at 0.059 ms/token. The defensible prefill figure is 102 s; the rest of the case is the context curve in §3.
- **Not that dedup improves solve rate.** 1–1 discordant at n=10 is a coin flip, and the mechanism producing it is the trajectory fork, not the lever.
- **Not that the cross-run 13.7% is a real-world saving.** Our harness triggers it (§4).
- **Not that `calm-run` pays off here.** A ClassEval suite runs in ~20 ms, so caching test executions saves ~40 ms on this bench. A repo with a 30-second suite is where it pays.

## Method notes a reviewer will ask about

- **`prefill_s` is derived, not measured.** Ollama does not split prefill from decode on the OpenAI-compatible endpoint and the agent does not stream, so there is no first-token boundary. §3 avoids the subtraction entirely by fitting measured request time against both token kinds; that fit recovers two constants it was never given.
- **Both A/B arms run through the same proxy**, `off` with tracing only. A control bypassing the proxy would have no trace at all, since Ollama reports no usage on a streamed request. Tracing relays bytes and writes a line.
- **The agent needed two fixes to work at all**: mini-swe-agent's default config drives the model with OpenAI tool calls, which a 7B does not emit (it exited `RepeatedFormatError` having touched nothing); and the 7B then wedged in `nano` until its cap expired. Both fixes are identical across arms.
- **Grow-only by construction.** The dedup memory is a G-Set keyed by content hash, so a rewrite is a pure function of content and the same message is rewritten identically every turn. That stability *is* the lever: a rewrite that moved would invalidate the prefix behind it, and at ~6 ms per prompt token one broken 17k-token prefix costs ~100 s — more than dedup saves across a whole task. Enforced by tests, not convention.

## Reproduce

```bash
python -m bench_agent.demo                    # every number, from the run dirs, no model needed
python -m bench_agent.make_results_md         # regenerate this document
```

*Background: this is built on a research project whose pre-registered hypothesis — that a coordination-free, content-addressed store raises class-level solve rate — came back **null** (v2 − C = +0.026, McNemar p = 1.000). That project is kept in full, failures included, in `README.md` and `PREREG.md`.*
